resources.string: How the spleen filters red blood cells
A qualitative view of one red cell route through normal human splenic red pulp. Sizes and timing are schematic.
The spleen sits beneath the left ribs. Its red pulp contains splenic cords and venous sinuses. The close-up shows red cells flowing through a cord toward a sinus.
A flexible red cell changes shape to squeeze through a narrow slit between cells in the sinus wall. It relaxes back toward its usual shape inside the sinus.
Less flexible red cells may stay behind
A red cell that deforms poorly may not fit through a slit. It can be held back on the cord side of the sinus wall.
A red pulp macrophage takes up a cell
A macrophage in the splenic red pulp can engulf a retained red cell and break it down.
As the red cell is broken down, iron is recovered from its hemoglobin. Released iron is carried in the blood and can be reused to make new red cells.
